findings.where: First screen, the blue field behind everything (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The field has diagonal white pinstripes across its whole area. This direction's lever is one flat field of house blue, and the tile's own Texture note says 'No texture: one flat field, no grain and no gradient'. The stripes put a busy, technical, blueprint-like hatch behind the headline, the lead and Mark's portrait.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for one blue field and a quiet ground, and Mark, who finds busy sites off-putting (brand sheet §6) and is not to be shown as 'techy'. The specimen also says the opposite of what the hero shows, so the founder can't tell which one is the proposal.

findings.where: First screen, the hero's topic pills (PPP Law, Infrastructure, Development banks, Governments, Risk allocation)
findings.fault: Five static facts are drawn as outlined capsules, the shape of filter chips or small buttons, and they sit right above the one action. parts.txt shows they do nothing when clicked. They also add a third row of things to the first screen, which should carry one message and one action.
findings.who_objects: A visitor from a development bank who clicks 'PPP Law' expecting Mark's PPP articles and gets nothing. The row of look-alike controls also competes with the email button for the eye.

findings.where: Article specimen, the bullets of the three-item list and the 'Streamlining the PPP Process…' link (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The list bullets and the lecture link are orange-red. That colour is not in the palette, which declares 'Four colours and no accent' and names house blue for links. Every other link on the page, such as 'Play again' and the email action, is blue, so one page now marks links in two colours.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose rule is that the house blue and grey are the only ink. Angélique, who can't tell from the tile what colour a link in an article should be. A reader, who loses the one consistent link signal.

findings.where: Article specimen: the list, and the image caption meeting the subhead (desktop and phone)
findings.fault: The rhythm breaks wherever the brief's test content appears. The list is set solid, with its lines almost touching and far tighter than the 19/30 body text above it. The caption 'A television studio interview…' sits flush against the subhead 'So, what are the key chapter topics?' with no space between them, so the caption reads as part of the heading.
findings.who_objects: The round-1 critics and the founder, who asked for type on a rhythm that holds when Angélique adds an image, caption, list or subhead. Here it holds for none of them. A reader also has trouble telling which text belongs to the photograph.

findings.where: Article specimen, the article title against the subhead
findings.fault: The subhead 'So, what are the key chapter topics?' is set as large and heavy as the title 'The World's Best Public-Private Partnership Law' on desktop, and larger than it on the phone. The section heading outranks the page heading.
findings.who_objects: A reader scanning the article, who takes the subhead as the start of a new article. Angélique, who would copy this scale onto every article.

findings.where: First screen, the giant ghost letters 'PPP' behind the headline (desktop; cropped behind the headline on phone)
findings.fault: A faint, oversized 'PPP' watermark sits under the first lines of the headline. It is a second decoration on top of the field. It muddies the large serif line that should stand alone, and it reads as a graphic gimmick.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for refined rather than novelty and for scale contrast rather than more elements. A first-time visitor, whose eye snags on the half-visible letters while reading Mark's line.

findings.fault: On the phone the portrait comes before the words. The first screen holds the nav, the photograph and its caption, and Mark's line starts only at the bottom edge. The lead and the email action are a full scroll down.
findings.who_objects: A visitor arriving from LinkedIn on a phone, who sees a face with no message or action until they scroll. The founder judges the first screen as the visitor's first screen.

findings.where: First screen, the nav lockup (mark, then 'Mark M. Moseley')
findings.fault: The mark comes first in reading order. Mark's name is set small to its right, at near-nav size, under the mark's visual weight, so the firm's mark leads rather than his name.
findings.who_objects: The founder, whose personal-advisor test asks that his name leads, with the logo beside it.

findings.where: Article specimen, the lecture row under the list ('Streamlining the PPP Process…', 'Lecture · 23 April 2026 · PDF')
findings.fault: A single related-publication row hangs off the end of the article under a hairline, with no heading. Read by proximity, it belongs to the article's list. Its 'PDF' label also suggests it opens a file directly rather than a page about the lecture.
findings.who_objects: A reader, who can't tell whether this is part of the article or a separate lecture. A procurement reader, who expects each lecture on its own page before the PDF.

findings.where: Article specimen title, the apostrophe in 'World's'
findings.fault: The title shows a tall, straight-looking apostrophe, while the subhead just below uses curly quotes (‘chapter topics’). Within one article the punctuation is set two ways.
findings.who_objects: A careful reader, and Mark, a lawyer who expects a well-set page. Few would notice.
